Pre-GA features are available "as is" and might have limited support. For more information, see the launch stage descriptions . Gemini Notebook Enterprise is a powerful tool for generating insights and summaries from your documents. This page describes the APIs that let you perform the following notebook management tasks programmatically: Create a notebook Retrieve a notebook List recently viewed notebooks Delete a notebook Share a notebook Before you begin Before you start working with your notebooks, do the following: Set up Gemini Notebook Enterprise . Get licenses for Gemini Notebook Enterprise and assign a license to your user account. Grant the Cloud NotebookLM User role ( roles/discoveryengine.notebookLmUser ) to your user account. In a local terminal or Cloud Shell , sign in to the Google Cloud CLI with your user credentials by running the gcloud auth login command: gcloud auth login Signing in with your user credentials ensures that gcloud auth print-access-token generates an access token for your user account. The projects.locations.notebooks REST API methods on this page require an authenticated user account with an active Gemini Notebook Enterprise license. Use the US multi-regional endpoint If your Gemini Notebook Enterprise subscription is in the US multi-region, you can send the requests on this page to the US multi-regional endpoint, discoveryengine.us.rep.googleapis.com . A multi-regional endpoint processes your requests and terminates TLS within the multi-region, so your request data stays in the US while it's in transit. Using this endpoint doesn't change where your notebooks are stored. For more information, see Regional and multi-regional API endpoints overview in the Google Cloud security guide. To use the US multi-regional endpoint, make the following changes to each request URL on this page: Replace the ENDPOINT_LOCATION -discoveryengine.googleapis.com host with discoveryengine.us.rep.googleapis.com . Set LOCATION to us . The rest of each request stays the same. To learn how you choose your subscription's multi-region, see Get a subscription . For the list of regional and multi-regional service endpoints, see Regional and multi-regional service endpoints in the Virtual Private Cloud guide. Create a notebook To create a new notebook, use the notebooks.create method. REST curl -X POST \ -H "Authorization:Bearer $( gcloud auth print-access-token ) " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ "https:// ENDPOINT_LOCATION -discoveryengine.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/ PROJECT_NUMBER /locations/ LOCATION /notebooks" \ -d '{ "title": " NOTEBOOK_TITLE ", }' Replace the following: ENDPOINT_LOCATION : the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following values: us for the US multi-region eu for the EU multi-region global for the Global location For more information, see Specify a multi-region for your data store . PROJECT_NUMBER : the number of your Google Cloud project. LOCATION : the geographic location of your data store, such as global . For more information, see Locations . NOTEBOOK_TITLE : a UTF-8 encoded string used as a title for the notebook that you want to create. If the request is successful, you should receive a JSON similar to the following. { "title" : " NOTEBOOK_TITLE " , "notebookId" : " NOTEBOOK_ID " , "emoji" : "" , "metadata" : { "userRole" : "PROJECT_ROLE_OWNER" , "isShared" : false , "isShareable" : true }, "name" : " NOTEBOOK_NAME " } Note the following: NOTEBOOK_ID : a unique ID to identify the created notebook. You need the notebook ID for other notebook management tasks, such as sharing or retrieving. NOTEBOOK_NAME : the complete resource name of the notebook. This field has the following pattern: projects/ PROJECT_NUMBER /locations/ LOCATION /notebooks/ NOTEBOOK_ID Access the created notebook and get its ID in a browser To access the created notebook and get its ID using a browser, do the following. Go to the Gemini Notebook Enterprise homepage that's available at one of the following URLs: If you're using a Google identity, go to: https://notebook.cloud.google.com/ LOCATION /?project= PROJECT_NUMBER If you're using a third-party identity, go to: https://notebook.cloud.google/ LOCATION /?project= PROJECT_NUMBER Select the created notebook. The URL of the selected notebook has the following pattern: If you're using a Google identity: https://notebook.cloud.google.com/ LOCATION /notebook/ NOTEBOOK_ID ?project= PROJECT_NUMBER If you're using a third-party identity: https://notebook.cloud.google/ LOCATION /notebook/ NOTEBOOK_ID ?project= PROJECT_NUMBER Note the URL and the notebook ID, which are useful for other notebook management tasks, such as sharing. Retrieve a notebook To retrieve a specific notebook using its notebook ID, use the notebooks.get method. REST curl -X GET \ -H "Authorization:Bearer $( gcloud auth print-access-token ) " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ "https:// ENDPOINT_LOCATION -discoveryengine.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/ PROJECT_NUMBER /locations/ LOCATION /notebooks/ NOTEBOOK_ID " Replace the following: ENDPOINT_LOCATION : the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following values: us for the US multi-region eu for the EU multi-region global for the Global location For more information, see Specify a multi-region for your data store . PROJECT_NUMBER : the number of your Google Cloud project. LOCATION : the geographic location of your data store, such as global . For more information, see Locations . NOTEBOOK_ID : the notebook's unique identifier that you received when you created the notebook. If the request is successful, you should get a JSON response similar to the following for an empty notebook. If you call this method after you add sources to your notebook, you receive details about all the sources added to the retrieved notebook. If you have configured CMEK details , you also receive CMEK-related information for the notebook. { "title" : " NOTEBOOK_TITLE " , "notebookId" : " NOTEBOOK_ID " , "emoji" : "" , "metadata" : { "userRole" : "PROJECT_ROLE_OWNER" , "isShared" : false , "isShareable" : true , "lastViewed" : " LAST_VIEWED_TIME " , "createTime" : " LAST_CREATED_TIME " }, "name" : " NOTEBOOK_NAME " } List recently viewed notebooks To get a list of all notebooks in a project that were recently viewed, use the notebooks.listRecentlyViewed method. By default, the response lists the last 500 notebooks. You can choose to paginate the responses with the pageSize query parameter. REST curl -X GET \ -H "Authorization:Bearer $( gcloud auth print-access-token ) " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ "https:// ENDPOINT_LOCATION -discoveryengine.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/ PROJECT_NUMBER /locations/ LOCATION /notebooks:listRecentlyViewed" Replace the following: ENDPOINT_LOCATION : the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following values: us for the US multi-region eu for the EU multi-region global for the Global location For more information, see Specify a multi-region for your data store . PROJECT_NUMBER : the number of your Google Cloud project. LOCATION : the geographic location of your data store, such as global . For more information, see Locations . If the request is successful, you should get a JSON response similar to the following. The response contains up to last 500 notebooks that a user accessed recently. { "notebooks" : [ { "title" : " NOTEBOOK_TITLE_1 " , "notebookId" : " NOTEBOOK_ID_1 " , "emoji" : "" , "metadata" : { "userRole" : "PROJECT_ROLE_OWNER" , "isShared" : false , "isShareable" : true , "lastViewed" : " LAST_VIEWED_TIME " , "createTime" : " LAST_CREATED_TIME " }, "name" : " NOTEBOOK_NAME_1 " }, { "title" : " NOTEBOOK_TITLE_2 " , "notebookId" : " NOTEBOOK_ID_2 " , "emoji" : "" , "metadata" : { "userRole" : "PROJECT_ROLE_OWNER" , "isShared" : false , "isShareable" : true , "lastViewed" : " LAST_VIEWED_TIME " , "createTime" : " LAST_CREATED_TIME " }, "name" : " NOTEBOOK_NAME_2 " } ] } Delete a notebook To delete a notebook, use the notebooks.batchDelete method. REST curl -X POST \ -H "Authorization:Bearer $( gcloud auth print-access-token ) " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ "https:// ENDPOINT_LOCATION -discoveryengine.googleapis.com/v1alpha/projects/ PROJECT_NUMBER /locations/ LOCATION /notebooks:batchDelete" \ -d '{ "names": [ " NOTEBOOK_NAME " ] }' Replace the following: ENDPOINT_LOCATION : the multi-region for your API request. Specify one of the following values: us for the US multi-region eu for the EU multi-region global for the Global location For more information, see Specify a multi-region for your data store . PROJECT_NUMBER : the number of your Google Cloud project. LOCATION : the geographic location of your data store, such as global . For more information, see Locations . NOTEBOOK_NAME : the complete resource name of the notebook to be deleted. This field has the pattern: projects/ PROJECT_NUMBER /locations/ LOCATION /notebooks/ NOTEBOOK_ID . If the request is successful, you receive an empty JSON object. If the notebook doesn't exist, you also receive an empty JSON object, so make sure to specify the notebook name correctly. documents.text: The Consensus API | The Consensus Help Center Skip to main content Back to Search Website Pricing Back to Search Website Pricing Search for articles... All Collections Explore features The Consensus API The Consensus API Written by Allison Elechko October 12, 2026 Table of contents The Consensus API lets you integrate Consensus search directly into your own applications, tools, and workflows. Use it to programmatically search academic research and retrieve relevant papers without needing to run each search manually in Consensus. API access is available directly from your Consensus account. Your API usage and Consensus MCP usage share the same monthly pool of calls. The number of calls included each month depends on your subscription tier. For full technical documentation, endpoints, parameters, and response details, read our API docs here . How to create an API key You can create and manage API keys from the API & MCP Dashboard. Click your profile icon (bottom-left corner) Select API & MCP Dashboard Open the ' Keys and Clients ' tab Click ' New key ' Give your API key a name so you can identify what you're using it for Create the key and copy it somewhere secure Your full API key is only shown once. Make sure you copy it when you create it. If you lose an API key, you won't be able to view it again. Instead, revoke the existing key and create a new one. Make your first API request Once you've created an API key, you can use it to authenticate requests to the Consensus API. To make a search request, you'll need three things: The Consensus search endpoint: https://api.consensus.app/v1/search Your API key, passed in the x-api-key request header A query parameter containing what you want to search for For example, if you want to search for research on whether creatine improves muscle strength, your request would send that question as the query to the Consensus search endpoint. If you're using a tool such as Postman, a programming language, or another application to make the request, add your Consensus API key as an x-api-key header. The API also supports filters that can help narrow your research, including publication date, study type, sample size, citation count, journal, academic field, country, open-access status, and more. For request examples and a full list of available parameters and responses, see the Consensus API Reference . Use the API to create and manage Threads In addition to standard paper search, the Consensus API can create and manage Threads. Threads are useful for more in-depth research tasks that require multi-step analysis, synthesis, and follow-up questions. Instead of only retrieving a list of papers, a Thread can generate a cited research answer with supporting papers and passages. With the Threads API, you can: Start a new Thread Poll a Thread until the response is ready Add a follow-up question to an existing Thread List historical Threads from your Consensus account Threads created through the API will also appear in your Consensus account. You can open them later in Consensus and continue working with them in the main interface. Thread usage is variable and counts toward your monthly API/MCP usage. A standard paper search typically uses fewer calls, while Threads may use more depending on the research mode, number of papers, and amount of work required. For implementation details and endpoint examples, see the Threads API documentation: https://docs.consensus.app/api-quickstart-threads Search and retrieve full text Consensus can use available full text, not just titles and abstracts, to help retrieve relevant papers. Paid users can also add include_full_text_chunks=true to a search request to return relevant passages from eligible open-access papers: Up to 3 passages per paper Up to 60 passages per request Each passage includes the section of the paper it came from If no eligible passage is available, full_text_chunks returns null Full-text retrieval is used when available on all plans. Returning full-text excerpts is available on Pro, Deep, Teams, and Enterprise plans. For request examples, full-text details, filters, and all available parameters, see the Consensus API documentation . How calls are counted API searches return up to 20 papers by default. You can use the page_size parameter to request more papers per page. Each call covers up to 100 papers: 1-100 papers = 1 call 101-200 papers = 2 calls 201-300 papers = 3 calls And so on, with each additional 100 papers counting as another call More advanced actions, such as creating a Consensus Thread, running a Pro or Deep Thread, or adding follow-up questions to a Thread, may use more calls depending on the amount of work required. Thread usage is variable because Consensus may run multiple research steps, search across more papers, read and synthesize results, and generate a cited response. You can view your usage from your profile > API & MCP Dashboard . The Usage tab shows activity by platform and tool, including searches, created Threads, Pro Threads, and Deep Threads. API and MCP usage limits API and MCP usage share one monthly pool of calls. Plan Included calls per month Maximum calls with additional usage ($0.05/call) Free 30 30 (no additional usage) Pro 500 1,000 Team 500 1,000 Enterprise 500 1,000 Deep 2,000 10,000 Additional usage costs $0.05 per call after you've used the calls included in your plan. Your usage resets on the 1st of each month. How to view your API and MCP usage To see your current usage: Click your profile icon in the bottom-left corner Select API & MCP Dashboard At the top of the dashboard, you'll see: Your current usage Any amount due for additional usage Your current plan and reset date The usage bar shows both the number of calls included in your plan and your total monthly call limit. The usage graph shows how your calls are split between API and MCP. You can view your usage for the last 7 days, last 30 days, or your current billing period. How to manage your API keys and MCP clients The Keys and Clients tab is where you manage both your API keys and MCP connections. API keys : you can create and revoke API keys MCP clients: you can connect Consensus to supported clients such as ChatGPT or Claude. If you've already connected a client, you'll see it here. How to enable additional usage Additional usage lets paid users continue making API and MCP calls after using all of the calls included in their plan. Additional usage is turned off by default. To enable it: Open the API & MCP Dashboard Select the settings control in the upper-right corner Under API & MCP settings, turn on Enable additional usage Save your changes Once enabled, calls beyond your plan's included amount are billed at $0.05 per call, up to your plan's maximum monthly call limit. You can turn additional usage off at any time. If you turn it off after you've already exceeded your included calls, you won't be able to make any more API or MCP calls until your usage resets. You'll still be billed for any additional calls made before you turned additional usage off. Free users cannot enable additional usage. To access additional usage, upgrade to a paid plan . Common API errors API Error message Cause Fix 401 - Invalid authentication credentials The API key is incorrect, revoked, or isn't being sent using the required header. Confirm you're using the correct API key in the x-api-key header. If you've lost the key, revoke it in the API & MCP Dashboard and create a new one. 402 - Billing past due Your subscription is past due, usually because a payment failed. API and MCP calls are paused until the billing issue is resolved. Update your payment method and resolve the outstanding payment to restore access. 429 - You've used all included {30, 500, 2,000, etc.} searches this month. Resets on {date}. You've used all of the API/MCP calls included in your plan. Paid users can enable additional usage from the API & MCP Dashboard, if they haven't reached their plan's maximum monthly call limit. Otherwise, wait until the reset date shown in the error message. 429 - Too many requests Requests are being sent faster than the current rate limit of one request per second. Slow down your requests and try again. Keep your API key secure Treat your API key like a password. Don't share it publicly or include it in publicly accessible client-side code, public repositories, screenshots, or other places where someone else could access it. If you believe a key has been exposed, revoke it from the API & MCP Dashboard and create a new one. You can manage your API keys, monitor API and MCP usage, review billing, and change your additional usage settings at any time from the API & MCP Dashboard. FAQs Where can I see my API/MCP billing history? Go to the API & MCP Dashboard, then click the Billing History tab. Do API and MCP have separate usage limits? No, your monthly usage limit is shared across API and MCP. What happens if I lose my API key? You won't be able to view the key again. Revoke the lost key and create a new one from the 'Keys and Clients' tab. Overview Prerequisites Create a Reducto account Get your API key Set your API key as an environment variable Install the SDK What we’re going to parse Parse the document Understanding the response Customizing the output Fastest path for coding agents Add Reducto MCP Server 1. Authenticate (one-time) 2. Add to your MCP client 3. Use it What’s next Troubleshooting Prerequisites 1 Create a Reducto account Sign up for a free account without leaving the docs. Signed in as Create account Sign in 2 Get your API key Create a key right here. Give it a name and copy it. It also shows up in Studio under API Keys . docs-quickstart Not created No key yet Reveal Create key The key fills into the code below. Manage keys in Studio under API Keys. Sign in to create a key here, or create one in Studio under API Keys. 3 Set your API key as an environment variable This allows the SDK to authenticate automatically without hardcoding the key in your code. export REDUCTO_API_KEY = "your-api-key" $env:REDUCTO_API_KEY = "your-api-key" 4 Install the SDK Choose your language and install the Reducto SDK. Python requires 3.8+. pip install reductoai npm install reductoai go get github.com/reductoai/reducto-go-sdk What we’re going to parse We’ll use a financial statement PDF that contains multiple tables, headers, account summaries, and formatted text. This is the kind of complex document that’s difficult to process manually but straightforward with Reducto. View the sample PDF in Studio or download it directly to follow along. What we want to extract: The portfolio value table with beginning and ending values Account information including account numbers and types Income summary broken down by tax category Top holdings with values and percentages By the end of this guide, you’ll have all of this data in structured JSON that you can use in your application. For structured field extraction (e.g., extracting specific account numbers or values into typed fields), see the /extract endpoint after completing this quickstart. Parse the document Now write the code that parses the financial statement. Here is what Reducto returns for it. from pathlib import Path from reducto import Reducto client = Reducto () upload = client . upload ( file = Path ( "fidelity-example.pdf" )) result = client . parse . run ( input = upload . file_id , settings = { "model" : "r-1" }) print ( f"Processed { result.usage.num_pages } pages" ) for chunk in result . result . chunks : print ( chunk . content ) for block in chunk . blocks : if block . type == "Table" : print ( f"Found table on page { block.bbox.page } " ) import fs from "node:fs" ; import Reducto from "reductoai" ; const client = new Reducto () ; const upload = await client . upload ({ file : fs . createReadStream ( "fidelity-example.pdf" ) }) ; const result = await client . parse . run ({ input : upload . file_id , settings : { model : "r-1" } }) ; console . log ( result . result . chunks [ 0 ] . content ) ; What you get back { "job_id" : "5df31070-8d98-..." , "usage" : { "num_pages" : 3 , "credits" : 4.0 } , "result" : { "chunks" : [{ "content" : "# *** SAMPLE STATEMENT ***..." , "blocks" : [{ "type" : "Table" , "bbox" : { "page" : 1 , "left" : 0.516 , ... } , "confidence" : "high" }] }] } , "studio_link" : "https://studio.reducto.ai/..." } Understanding the response Here’s what we got back from parsing our financial statement: { "job_id" : "5df31070-8d98-4caa-9a5b-c5c511a03f71" , "duration" : 11.35 , "usage" : { "num_pages" : 3 , "credits" : 4.0 } , "result" : { "chunks" : [ { "content" : "# *** SAMPLE STATEMENT *** 
 For informational purposes only 

 Fidelity 
 INVESTMENTS 

 ## Your Portfolio Value: 

 $274,222.20 

 | | This Period | Year-to-Date | 
 |-|-|-| 
 | Beginning Portfolio Value | $253,221.83 | $232,643.16 | 
 | Additions | 59,269.64 | 121,433.55 |..." , "blocks" : [ { "type" : "Title" , "content" : "*** SAMPLE STATEMENT *** 
 For informational purposes only" , "bbox" : { "page" : 1 , "left" : 0.351 , "top" : 0.029 , "width" : 0.296 , "height" : 0.057 } , "confidence" : "high" } , { "type" : "Section Header" , "content" : "Your Portfolio Value:" , "bbox" : { "page" : 1 , "left" : 0.517 , "top" : 0.163 , "width" : 0.153 , "height" : 0.015 } , "confidence" : "high" } , { "type" : "Table" , "content" : "| | This Period | Year-to-Date | 
 |-|-|-| 
 | Beginning Portfolio Value | $253,221.83 | $232,643.16 | 
 | Additions | 59,269.64 | 121,433.55 | 
 | Subtractions | -45,430.74 | -98,912.58 | 
 | Transaction Costs, Fees & Charges | -139.77 | -625.87 | 
 | Change in Investment Value* | 7,161.47 | 19,058.07 | 
 | Ending Portfolio Value** | $274,222.20 | $274,222.20 |" , "bbox" : { "page" : 1 , "left" : 0.516 , "top" : 0.261 , "width" : 0.444 , "height" : 0.158 } , "confidence" : "high" } ] } ] } , "studio_link" : "https://studio.reducto.ai/job/5df31070-8d98-4caa-9a5b-c5c511a03f71" } Key fields: Field What it contains job_id Unique identifier for this job. Use it to retrieve results later or debug in Studio. usage.num_pages Number of pages that were processed. usage.credits Credits consumed by this request. chunks Logical sections of the document, optimized for feeding into LLMs. chunks[].content The full text content of this chunk. chunks[].blocks Individual elements (tables, headers, text) with their types and positions. blocks[].type What kind of element this is: Title , Table , Section Header , Text , Figure , etc. blocks[].bbox Bounding box with normalized coordinates (0-1) showing where this element appears on the page. studio_link Direct link to view this job in Reducto Studio for visual debugging. Customizing the output r-1 needs no extra settings. The options you may want change the shape of the output, not its quality: result = client . parse . run ( input = upload . file_id , settings = { "model" : "r-1" , "page_range" : { "start" : 1 , "end" : 5 }} , formatting = { "table_output_format" : "html" } , retrieval = { "chunking" : { "chunk_mode" : "variable" }} , ) formatting.table_output_format : dynamic (default), html , md , json , or csv . retrieval.chunking.chunk_mode : split the output into chunks for RAG. settings.page_range : parse only some pages. For word-level bounding boxes, add Parse citations . See Parse options for the full list. Fastest path for coding agents If you are using Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or another coding agent, start here. This path avoids Studio clicks and extra docs navigation. Set REDUCTO_API_KEY . Choose one interface: Local file or folder: use the Reducto CLI . Agent tool calling: use the Reducto MCP server . Application code: use the Python, Node.js, Go, or cURL examples below. Parse the sample PDF first, then replace the URL or file path with your document. pip install reducto-cli reducto login curl -L -o fidelity-example.pdf https : //cdn.reducto.ai/samples/fidelity-example.pdf reducto parse ./fidelity-example.pdf from reducto import Reducto client = Reducto () result = client . parse . run ( input = "https://cdn.reducto.ai/samples/fidelity-example.pdf" , settings = { "model" : "r-1" }) print ( result . job_id ) print ( result . result . chunks [ 0 ] . content [ : 1000 ]) import Reducto from "reductoai" ; const client = new Reducto () ; const result = await client . parse . run ({ input : "https://cdn.reducto.ai/samples/fidelity-example.pdf" , settings : { model : "r-1" } , }) ; console . log ( result . job_id ) ; console . log ( result . result . chunks [ 0 ] . content . slice ( 0 , 1000 )) ; curl -X POST "https://platform.reducto.ai/parse" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDUCTO_API_KEY " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"input":"https://cdn.reducto.ai/samples/fidelity-example.pdf","settings":{"model":"r-1"}}' Tip For MCP, install once with uvx mcp-server-reducto --login , then ask the agent to call parse_document(document_url="https://cdn.reducto.ai/samples/fidelity-example.pdf") . Add Reducto MCP Server 1. Authenticate (one-time) uvx mcp-server-reducto --login This opens your browser to approve access. Your API key is saved to ~/.reducto/config.yaml . 2. Add to your MCP client Claude Code: claude mcp add reducto -- uvx mcp-server-reducto Claude Desktop : edit ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json : { "mcpServers" : { "reducto" : { "command" : "uvx" , "args" : [ "mcp-server-reducto" ] } } } Cursor : edit .cursor/mcp.json : { "mcpServers" : { "reducto" : { "command" : "uvx" , "args" : [ "mcp-server-reducto" ] } } } VS Code : edit .vscode/mcp.json : { "servers" : { "reducto" : { "command" : "uvx" , "args" : [ "mcp-server-reducto" ] } } } 3. Use it The server provides these tools: Tool What it does upload_file Upload a local file or URL to Reducto (returns reducto:// URL) parse_document Parse a document into structured text, tables, figures extract_data Extract structured JSON from a document using a schema split_document Segment a document into labeled sections classify_document Categorize a document type edit_document Fill forms or modify a PDF/DOCX Local files: Use upload_file first, e.g. upload_file("./report.pdf") , then pass the returned reducto:// URL to other tools. Chain operations: parse_document returns a job_id . Pass jobid://<job_id> to extract_data or split_document to skip re-parsing. What’s next Now that you can parse documents, explore the other Reducto endpoints: /extract Define a JSON schema and extract specific fields from your documents. /split Divide long documents into sections based on content type. /edit Fill PDF forms and modify DOCX documents programmatically. /parse (async) Process documents asynchronously with webhooks for high-volume workloads. Troubleshooting 401 Unauthorized error This means your API key is missing or invalid. Check that the REDUCTO_API_KEY environment variable is set correctly and that the key hasn’t expired

Service users (recommended for automation) How it works Service user scopes Session attribution with create_as_user_id Key properties Personal access tokens Legacy authentication (deprecated) Security best practices Troubleshooting 401 Unauthorized 403 Forbidden 404 Not Found Next steps Concepts Authentication Copy page Copy page Understand principals, tokens, and how to authenticate with the Devin API Copy page Copy page The Devin API uses a principal + token model. A principal is who you are (your identity), and a token is how you prove it (your credential). Understanding this distinction is the key to choosing the right authentication method for your use case. Principals & tokens Principal Token Description Service User (non-human) Service User API Key For automated integrations and CI/CD pipelines User (human) Personal Access Token (PAT) For human programmatic access under your own identity All API credentials use the cog_ prefix format. Include your token in the Authorization header of every request: curl -X GET "https://api.devin.ai/v3/organizations/ $DEVIN_ORG_ID /sessions" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer cog_your_token_here" The key distinction is which principal the token authenticates as : A Service User API Key authenticates as the service user — the service user’s identity, permissions, and org memberships apply. A Personal Access Token authenticates as the human user who created it — that user’s identity, permissions, and org memberships apply. Personal access token or service user? Personal access token Service user API key Acts as You A separate non-human identity Permissions Exactly yours, in every organization you have access to The role you give the service user, in the organizations it is added to Scope Your account. Each request names the organization Created at the organization or enterprise level Audit trail Attributed to you Attributed to the service user, even when it creates a session on someone’s behalf with create_as_user_id Lifecycle Tied to you. Revoked automatically if you leave the account Not tied to any person, so it survives team changes Best for Personal scripts, local tooling, the Devin CLI and desktop apps CI/CD, production integrations, shared automation Rule of thumb: if the integration should keep working after you leave the team or change roles, use a service user. If it should do exactly what you can do, as you, use a PAT. Service users (recommended for automation) Service users are non-human accounts designed for API integrations. They can be assigned specific permissions via RBAC and added to organizations independently of human users. How it works Provision a service user in Settings > Devin API ( Service users tab) for an organization, or Enterprise settings > Devin API ( Service users tab) for the enterprise Assign a role that controls which endpoints the service user can access. You pick a role from a dropdown, not individual permissions Choose an expiration — it defaults to 30 days; the other options are 7 days, 90 days, and, where your account allows it, Never Copy the API key — the key starts with cog_ and is shown only once, right after provisioning Use the key in the Authorization header of every API request curl -X POST "https://api.devin.ai/v3/organizations/ $DEVIN_ORG_ID /sessions" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $DEVIN_API_KEY " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"prompt": "Create a simple Python script"}' Service user scopes Scope Created in API access Use case Organization Settings > Devin API > Service users /v3/organizations/* Session management, knowledge, playbooks, secrets Enterprise Enterprise settings > Devin API > Service users /v3/enterprise/* + /v3/organizations/* Cross-org management, analytics, audit logs, billing Find your organization ID at the top of the Settings > Devin API page. Session attribution with create_as_user_id Service users are separate identities from human users. By default, sessions created by a service user are attributed to the service user itself. To create sessions on behalf of a specific user , pass the create_as_user_id parameter when creating a session. The session will appear in that user’s session list and count toward their usage. This requires the ImpersonateOrgSessions permission on the service user’s role. Key properties Keys start with cog_ and are shown only once at creation time Service users appear separately from human users in audit logs Permissions are controlled via RBAC — assign only what the integration needs Enterprise service users inherit org-level permissions across all organizations For detailed setup instructions, see the Teams quick start or Enterprise quick start . Personal access tokens Personal Access Tokens (PATs) allow human users to authenticate programmatically under their own identity. When you use a PAT, the API sees you — your permissions, your org memberships, and your audit trail. This is useful when you want to make API calls as yourself (e.g., personal scripts, local tooling) rather than through a shared service user. A PAT is not scoped to an organization or an enterprise. It belongs to you within your account and works in every organization you have access to. Each request names an organization in the URL, and your role in that organization decides what the request can do. For enterprise accounts, PATs are governed by an enterprise-wide policy (disabled by default) that enterprise admins configure — including an approval workflow and mandatory token expiration. For more details, see Personal Access Tokens . Legacy authentication (deprecated) Legacy API keys are deprecated. Use API v3 with service user authentication. See the migration guide . Legacy API keys are used with the v1 and v2 APIs. They continue to work during the deprecation period but do not support new features like RBAC, session attribution, or cursor-based pagination. Key type Prefix Used with Description Personal API key apk_user_ v1, v2 Tied to a user account, inherits user permissions Service API key apk_ v1 Organization-scoped, for automation Where to generate: Settings > API Keys Security best practices Never share API keys in publicly accessible areas such as GitHub repositories, client-side code, or logs. Store keys securely : Use environment variables or secret management systems Rotate keys regularly : Generate new keys and revoke old ones periodically Use service users for automation : Prefer service users over personal keys for production Apply least privilege : Grant only the minimum permissions required Monitor usage : Review audit logs for unexpected API activity Revoke compromised keys immediately : If a key is exposed, revoke it and generate a new one. In Settings > Devin API , a service user’s key has no revoke or rotate button: use Delete service user on its row, which stops the key immediately, then provision a new one. Enterprises can also revoke or rotate a service user’s key through the API (beta) Troubleshooting 401 Unauthorized Possible causes: Invalid or expired API key Missing Authorization header Incorrect Bearer token format Using a legacy API key ( apk_ / apk_user_ ) with the Devin MCP — only cog_ -prefixed keys are supported Solution: Verify your API key is correct and properly formatted in the Authorization header. For MCP usage, ensure you are using a service user API key (not a legacy key). 403 Forbidden Possible causes: API key doesn’t have required permissions Using the wrong key type for the endpoint (e.g., legacy key with v3 endpoints) Attempting to access resources outside your scope Solution: Ensure your service user has the correct role and permissions For legacy v2 endpoints: ensure you have the Enterprise Admin role For legacy v1 endpoints: verify you have access to the organization 404 Not Found Possible causes: Incorrect API endpoint URL Resource doesn’t exist or you don’t have access Solution: Verify the endpoint URL and that the resource exists. Aug 1, 2026 How do I access Higgsfield via CLI? Higgsfield 3 min Copy page CLI and Skills is how Higgsfield integrates with coding agents. The difference from MCP: MCP is a full connection for chat agents that exposes all tools with free parameter selection, while CLI and Skills is optimized for coding agents, where each skill has a defined structure that reduces token overhead and produces consistent output. Accessing Higgsfield through the CLI falls under the Developer Terms in the Terms of Use : keep your session secure, and you're responsible for what a coding agent generates through your account. Both use the same Higgsfield account and plan credits with no API key (API keys belong to the Higgsfield API, a separate developer product), and Unlimited models and free generations don't apply to either. See the setup guide and full skill list on the Skills landing page . When should I use CLI instead of MCP? When should I use CLI instead of MCP? Criteria CLI + Skills MCP Best for Coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) Chat agents (Claude web, Cowork) Token overhead Minimal Full schema per call Output format Structured through skills Agent picks parameters freely Credits Same account, same rates Same account, same rates Unlimited models No No API key required No No How do I set up CLI + Skills? Install skills: run npx skills add higgsfield-ai/skills . This pulls three skills: generate, soul, and product-photoshoot. Sign in: run higgsfield auth login . No API key needed. Generate: in your coding agent, call /higgsfield:generate or say "Generate an image with Higgsfield." The agent picks the skill and runs it. Compatible with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and other agents that support Skills or MCP. What are the three Skills? generate , image and video generation from any Higgsfield model (Soul, Nano Banana Pro for images; Seedance, Kling, Veo for video), up to 4K. The agent selects a model automatically, or you can specify one. soul , train a Soul character from photos. The skill handles upload, training, and naming. See How do I create and use a Soul ID character? product-photoshoot , turn a product link or images into studio-quality product shots and video ads. Works for physical products and apps. Image presets: What are the three Skills? Preset What it generates product_shot Product on a neutral, studio, or catalog background lifestyle_scene Product in a real-world environment closeup_product_with_person Tight crop with hands or partial face and product pinterest_pin Vertical 2:3 Pinterest-native format hero_banner Wide-format banner for website, email, or campaign social_carousel 3 to 10 connected slides for Instagram or LinkedIn ad_creative_pack Coordinated set of static ad variations virtual_model_tryout Product worn or used by an AI-rendered model conceptual_product Surreal, CGI-style, or levitating product restyle Transform an existing image's aesthetic Video presets: UGC, Tutorial, Unboxing, Hyper Motion, Product Review, TV Spot, Wild Card, UGC Virtual Try On, Pro Virtual Try On. Got any questions left? What is the difference between CLI Skills and the Skills inside Supercomputer? Two separate systems with the same name. CLI Skills are installed via npx skills add higgsfield-ai/skills for coding agents. Supercomputer Skills are built-in functions called with "/" inside the Supercomputer chat. They are not interchangeable. Do I need both CLI and MCP? No. Use MCP for chat agents like Claude web, and CLI for coding agents like Claude Code or Cursor. Which models are available through CLI? All Higgsfield models. The agent selects automatically unless you specify one. My reference images aren't being passed to the generation. What do I do? Update to the latest CLI version by re-running npx skills add higgsfield-ai/skills . Earlier versions had an issue with passing references; current versions pass all references, including images, correctly. Do I need to reinstall the skills after updates? Run npx skills add higgsfield-ai/skills again to pull the latest version. Where do CLI generations appear? In your Assets on higgsfield.ai , the same as web and MCP generations. How to Connect Higgsfield to Claude or ChatGPT Higgsfield Explore Image Video Audio MCP API Cinema Studio Genjutsu Top Short Drama New Miracle Soon Contests Shorts New Ads Studio New GPU New Playable Supercomputer Community Academy Plugins Canvas Higgsfield New drops Drops Home Image Video Audio MCP Agentic Studios Community Contests Learn More Creator Hub Back Help center / Integrations / How do I connect Higgsfield to Claude, ChatGPT, or another AI agent? Aug 1, 2026 How do I connect Higgsfield to Claude, ChatGPT, or another AI agent? Higgsfield 7 min Copy page Higgsfield connects to Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, and other MCP-compatible agents, with no API key. In Claude, add a custom connector with the URL https://mcp.higgsfield.ai/mcp . In ChatGPT, add the Higgsfield Plugin from the Plugins Directory. In Cursor, add Higgsfield from the marketplace. In Claude Code, OpenClaw, and Hermes, the agent installs the Higgsfield CLI. An active paid subscription is required. What do I need before connecting? An active Higgsfield subscription and an account in the AI agent: Claude (claude.ai or Claude Desktop), ChatGPT, Cursor, or any other MCP-compatible client. No API key or additional setup is needed. Which agents can I connect? Which agents can I connect? Agent How it connects Claude (claude.ai and Claude Desktop) Custom connector with the MCP server URL ChatGPT Official Higgsfield Plugin from the Plugins Directory Cursor Higgsfield from the marketplace Claude Code, OpenClaw, Hermes Higgsfield CLI, set up by the agent itself Any other MCP-compatible client MCP server URL in the agent's settings How do I connect in Claude? Open claude.ai or Claude Desktop and go to Settings → Connectors . Click Add custom connector . Name it Higgsfield and paste the MCP server URL: https://mcp.higgsfield.ai/mcp Click Connect : a Higgsfield authorization window opens. Sign in to your Higgsfield account and authorize. If you're already logged in on higgsfield.ai , this step is automatic. Return to Claude: the Higgsfield connector appears in your active connectors list. How do I connect in ChatGPT? ChatGPT uses the official Higgsfield Plugin instead of a manual URL: Open the Plugins Directory in ChatGPT, or go to higgsfield.ai/mcp and select Add Higgsfield plugin . Find Higgsfield and select Add . Sign in to your Higgsfield account and authorize. Audio generation and the Website Building skill aren't available in ChatGPT: for those, use higgsfield.ai or Claude. How do I connect in Cursor? In Cursor, open Customize → Marketplace and find Higgsfield. Click Add and sign in to your Higgsfield account. Ask Cursor to generate an image or video. How do I connect in Claude Code, OpenClaw, or Hermes? These agents connect through the Higgsfield CLI, which the agent installs itself. Copy and send this message to your agent: “Set up Higgsfield for me so I can generate images and videos from here. 1. Install the CLI: run npm i -g @higgsfield/cli . 2. Authenticate: run higgsfield auth login and complete the sign-in in the browser it opens. 3. Install the companion skills: run npx skills add higgsfield-ai/skills . Once that's done, let me know when it's ready.” Complete the sign-in in the browser window that opens, then ask the agent to generate an image or video. For more detail, see How do I access Higgsfield via CLI? What can each agent do? What can each agent do? Criteria Claude ChatGPT Cursor Claude Code, OpenClaw, Hermes Image and video generation ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Soul characters ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ Audio generation ✓ ✕ ✓ ✓ Website Building skill ✓ ✕ ✓ ✓ Results saved to Assets ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ What are Higgsfield skills? Skills are preset workflows for common tasks. You describe the result you want, and the skill goes through the intermediate steps (concept, script, individual generations) without separate prompts for each one. The full list is at higgsfield.ai/skills . What are Higgsfield skills? Skill category What it does Marketing Launch ads and campaigns UGC Factory Create creator-led product videos, including Product Review UGC and SaaS UGC Faceless Content Factory Create viral faceless videos, including Stickman Cartoon and Editorial Motion Graphics Utility Edit, repurpose, and optimize Motion & Design Design and animate visuals Website Building Design and ship websites (not available in ChatGPT) How do I verify the connection is working? Start a new conversation and ask "What is my Higgsfield credit balance?" or "List my recent Higgsfield generations." The agent will call the Higgsfield tools and return your account data. If it responds without calling any tools, check your connectors or plugins list and reconnect. What can I generate through MCP? What can I generate through MCP? Operation Available via MCP Image and video generation (all models) ✓ Image and video upscaling ✓ Background removal (image and video) ✓ Expand image (outpaint) and expand video (reframe) ✓ Kling 3.0 Motion Control ✓ Soul characters and reference Elements ✓ Audio: voiceover, voice cloning, voice change, video dubbing ✓ Personal Clipper (YouTube videos into short clips) ✓ Check credit balance, list generations and uploads ✓ Unlimited model access ✕ Free generations ✕ Every generation through a connected agent deducts credits, regardless of your plan. See What is Higgsfield MCP, and how is it different from the web? How do I give the agent the right instructions? The agent selects a model automatically if you don't name one. You can also specify exactly what to use: Specify the model. "Generate a video using Seedance of a person walking through a forest at sunrise, realistic motion, camera tracking close." Use a Soul character. "Generate an image using my Soul character [name] in an editorial fashion setting, studio lighting, neutral background." Use a reference Element. "Generate an image with my element [name] in a rooftop cafe at golden hour." Elements are reusable references for characters, environments, and props, and you can use several in one prompt. Audio. "Generate a voiceover for this text in a warm professional tone: [text]." Check balance before generating. "What is my current Higgsfield credit balance?" Approve before spending. At the start of a session, say: "Before generating anything, tell me the credit cost and wait for my confirmation." How do I pass a reference image through MCP? The agent can't read images attached to the chat itself: reference files reach Higgsfield through a separate upload step that the agent opens for you. Just tell the agent what you want to use, and it picks the right path. A file on your device. Say something like "I have a photo on my computer I want to use as the character reference." The agent opens the Higgsfield upload window right in the conversation: choose the file there, and it uploads directly to your Higgsfield account. Once the upload is confirmed, describe its role in the prompt: "Use the uploaded image as the character reference and generate a video of them walking through Times Square at night." An image from the web. Paste the direct image URL into the chat and describe its role: "Import this image and use it as the style reference: [link]." The agent imports it into your Higgsfield uploads and passes it to the generation. A past generation or a saved character. Nothing to upload: reference a previous Higgsfield generation ("use the portrait I generated earlier as the start frame"), a reference Element by name, or a trained Soul character by name, and the agent passes it to the model directly. For Kling 3.0 Motion Control, you need two inputs: a character image and a motion reference video. The agent opens the upload window for each, and you describe which is which: "The image is the character, the video is the motion reference." If the agent asks you to attach a file to the chat instead of opening the upload window, remind it: "Open the Higgsfield upload window for my file." Where do my generations appear? All generations from connected agents land in your Assets at higgsfield.ai , exactly like generations made on the web, tagged with the MCP source so you can filter by it. Results typically appear within 60 seconds of the job completing. Common issues and fixes "Authorization with the MCP server failed." The authentication token has expired. In Claude, go to Settings → Connectors → Higgsfield , click Disconnect , then reconnect and re-authorize. In ChatGPT, reconnect the plugin from Settings → Plugins → Higgsfield . The connector appears connected, but the agent isn't calling Higgsfield tools. Start a new conversation and mention Higgsfield explicitly. Check whether the connector is toggled on in the current conversation: some interfaces have a per-conversation toggle. "MCP HTTP exchange failed" in Cursor or another agent. A transient connection error: retry the request. If it persists, disconnect and reconnect the MCP server in your agent's settings. Got any questions left? Can I connect Higgsfield in several agents at the same time? Yes. The same Higgsfield account can be connected in Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, and other agents simultaneously. How is the ChatGPT connection different from Claude? In Claude, Higgsfield connects as a custom connector with the MCP server URL. In ChatGPT, it's an official plugin you add from the Plugins Directory: no URL to paste. Both use the same account and the same credits. Do generations in connected agents use my Higgsfield credits? Yes. Every generation through MCP, the ChatGPT plugin, or the CLI deducts credits at standard rates. Unlimited access and free generations apply only on higgsfield.ai . Can I build websites from ChatGPT? No. The Website Building skill isn't available in ChatGPT. Use Claude, Cursor, or a CLI-based agent instead. My generation isn't showing up. What do I do? Wait up to 60 seconds, then check Manage Account → Usage to confirm the job ran. If credits were deducted but no output is visible, contact support with the generation ID and the time of generation. Can I limit how many credits the agent uses per session? There's no native credit cap. Instruct the agent in the conversation: "Do not spend more than X credits. Always ask for approval before generating." This is a prompt-level instruction, not a hard limit. How do I disconnect? In Claude: Settings → Connectors → Higgsfield → Disconnect. In ChatGPT: Settings → Plugins → Higgsfield. In CLI-based agents, log out through the CLI. Share Feedback Was this article helpful? It takes a mermaid definition file as input and generates an SVG/PNG/PDF file as output. There's basic support for converting mermaid code blocks embedded within Markdown files. Installation npm install -g @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli Usage Convert Mermaid mmd Diagram File To SVG mmdc -i input.mmd -o output.svg Note See Alternative installations if you don't want to install the package globally. Locate how to call the mmdc executable for your preferred method i.e. Docker, Yarn, NPM, local install, etc. Examples Create A PNG With A Dark Theme And Transparent Background mmdc -i input.mmd -o output.png -t dark -b transparent Adding custom icon packs to Mermaid mermaid-cli supports two different ways to add custom icon packs to mermaid : Icon packs installed via npm install , e.g. @iconify-json/logos . These can be used via the --iconPacks @iconify-json/logos . Icon packs accessible via URI. These can either be URLs or local file:// URIs to local files. For example, to download the above @iconify-json/logos package from a CDN like jsDelivr , you can do --iconPacksAndUrls logos#https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@iconify-json/logos@1.2.14/icons.json . Animating an SVG file with custom CSS The --cssFile option can be used to inline some custom CSS. It's passed to Mermaid's themeCSS config option . Please see ./test-positive/flowchart1.css for an example of a CSS file that has animations. Warning : Inline CSS files may be blocked by your browser, depending on the HTTP Content-Security-Policy header of the website that hosts your SVG. mmdc --input test-positive/flowchart1.mmd --cssFile test-positive/flowchart1.css -o docs/animated-flowchart.svg Example output: docs/animated-flowchart.svg Selecting the size of the created file The --size value can be used to attempt to create a PNG of the given size, by setting a max-width on the SVG. For narrow diagrams, this would decide set the max height, and for wide diagrams, this will set the max width. For example, the following command will create a PNG of height 4000px: mmdc --input test-positive/flowchart1.mmd --size 4000 -o output.png ![Note] This may not work with all diagram types and/or may require useMaxWidth: true to be set in the diagram's config. Transform a markdown file with mermaid diagrams mmdc -i readme.template.md -o readme.md This command transforms a markdown file itself. The mermaid-cli will find the mermaid diagrams, create SVG files from them and refer to those in the markdown output. This: ### Some markdown ``` mermaid graph [....] ``` ### Some more markdown ``` mermaid sequenceDiagram [....] ``` ### Mermaid with custom title/desc ``` mermaid graph accTitle: My title here accDescr: My description here A-->B ``` Becomes: ### Some markdown ![ diagram ] ( ./readme-1.svg ) ### Some more markdown ![ diagram ] ( ./readme-2.svg ) ### Mermaid with custom title/desc ![ My description here ] ( ./readme-3.svg " My title here ") Piping from stdin You can easily pipe input from stdin. This example shows how to use a heredoc to send a diagram as stdin to mermaid-cli (mmdc). cat << EOF | mmdc --input - graph TD A[Client] --> B[Load Balancer] EOF See All Available Options mmdc -h Alternative installations Use Docker/Podman: docker pull minlag/mermaid-cli or pull from Github Container Registry docker pull ghcr.io/mermaid-js/mermaid-cli/mermaid-cli or e.g. version 8.8.0 docker pull minlag/mermaid-cli:8.8.0 The container looks for input files in /data . So for example, if you have a diagram defined on your system in /path/to/diagrams/diagram.mmd , you can use the container to generate an SVG file as follows: docker run --rm -u ` id -u ` : ` id -g ` -v /path/to/diagrams:/data minlag/mermaid-cli -i diagram.mmd Or, if using Podman , instead do: podman run --userns keep-id --user ${UID} --rm -v /path/to/diagrams:/data:z ghcr.io/mermaid-js/mermaid-cli/mermaid-cli -i diagram.mmd The key differences in the podman command versus the docker command are: The addition of the --userns keep-id argument. This allows the container to keep the same UID as the current user's UID in the container namespace instead of mapping to a subuid. To learn more, see the userns=mode documentation . The addition of :z to the end of the volume mapping. This instructs podman to relabel the files in the volume with the SELinux label container_file_t , which allows processes in the container to access the files. See the "Labeling Volume Mounts" section of podman-run (1) for more info. In previous version, the input files were mounted in /home/mermaidcli . You can restore this behaviour with the --workdir option: docker run [...] --workdir=/home/mermaidcli minlag/mermaid-cli [...] Use Node.JS API It's possible to call mermaid-cli via a Node.JS API. Please be aware that the NodeJS API is not covered by semver , as mermaid-cli follows mermaid 's versioning. import { run } from "@mermaid-js/mermaid-cli" ; await run ( "input.mmd" , "output.svg" , // {optional options}, ) ; Install locally Some people are having issues installing this tool globally. Installing it locally is an alternative solution: npm install @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli ./node_modules/.bin/mmdc -h Run with npx npx is installed by default with NPM. It downloads and runs commands at the same time. To use Mermaid CLI with npx, you need to use the -p flag because the package name is different than the command it installs ( mmdc ). npx -p @mermaid-js/mermaid-cli mmdc -h Install with brew Warning This method of installation is no longer supported. For more details, see the discussion . An old version of mermaid-cli can be installed with brew. brew install mermaid-cli Known issues Linux sandbox issue Docker permission denied issue How to setup up mermaid to use already installed chromium? For contributors Contributions are welcome. See the contribution guide . documents.text: Authentication — Grain Developers / API Docs MCP Docs ↗ grain.com ↗ Overview Authentication Versions Rate Limits Endpoints Uploads Hooks 2025-10-31 Endpoints Authentication Authenticating Calls To authenticate API calls, the client must add the following header: Copy Authorization : Bearer TOKEN where TOKEN is obtained by one of the methods below. Token Types There are three types of tokens which can have one of two access scopes. Type Scope Personal Access Token ( PAT ) personal Generated manually from the integrations page . Doesn't expire, and can be revoked at any time. Workspace Access Token ( WAT ) workspace Generated manually from the integrations page . Doesn't expire, and can be revoked at any time. OAuth Token personal , workspace Issued through the OAuth2 Flow . Expires, must be refreshed. Scope personal Provides the same access level as the user who authorized the token. workspace Provides FULL DATA ACCESS of the workspace. Can be generated by workspace admins only. NOTE: The workspace scope is not available on all plans. Check https://grain.com/pricing to see if your plan includes Workspace API. Tokens with the personal scope, including Personal Access Tokens, also authenticate the Grain MCP server at https://api.grain.com/_/mcp . Tokens with the workspace scope are not accepted by the MCP server. OAuth2 Flow This authentication method is for developers building integrations with Grain to be used by any Grain users. The API supports a standard OAuth2 Authorization Code flow, including the PKCE extension for client-side only authentication. At least one redirect URI is required to register a new client. For browser-based client applications, a list of CORS origins can also be added. Authorization Code Step 1 Obtain the client_id and client_secret (only for server-side applications) credentials. Step 2 Open the url https://grain.com/_/public-api/oauth2/authorize with the following query params. Param client_id Obtained separately in Step 1 redirect_uri Must exactly match a registered redirect URI. On localhost , 127.0.0.1 and [::1] , any port matches response_type Must be code state Optional. Grain returns it unchanged in Step 4 . PKCE already protects the flow, so state is only needed if your client relies on it code_challenge A random string, hashed with SHA256 and base64 URL encoded code_challenge_method Must be S256 scopes personal or workspace . Defaults to personal Step 3 If the user is not already signed in to Grain, they will be prompted to sign in. After being authenticated, the user will be prompted to confirm the OAuth2 connection. Step 4 The user will be redirected to redirect_uri from Step 2 with the code query param, and state if you sent one. Step 5 Make a POST request to generate the token. See OAuth2 Generate Token Diagram sequenceDiagram participant you as You actor user as User participant grain as Grain Note right of you: Step 1 you-->>grain: Request Client ID & Secret (manually) grain-->>you: Client ID & Secret Note right of you: Step 2 user->>you: Requests OAuth you->>user: Open or Redirects to oauth2/authorize user->>grain: oauth2/authorize Note left of grain: Step 3 grain->>user: Requests login user->>grain: Login grain->>user: Requests Confirm OAuth user->>grain: Confirms Note left of grain: Step 4 grain->>user: Redirects to redirect_uri w/code user->>you: redirect_uri w/code Note right of you: Step 5 you->>grain: POST oauth2/token w/code grain->>you: access_token & refresh_token Note right of you: Refresh you->>grain: POST oauth2/token w/refresh_token grain->>you: access_token & refresh_token Client ID Metadata Document Public clients, such as MCP clients and native apps, can skip Step 1 by using an HTTPS URL as their client_id . That URL must serve a JSON Client ID Metadata Document describing the client. Copy { "client_id" : "https://app.example.com/oauth/client.json" , "client_name" : "Example App" , "redirect_uris" : [ "https://app.example.com/oauth/callback" ] , "grant_types" : [ "authorization_code" , "refresh_token" ] , "response_types" : [ "code" ] , "token_endpoint_auth_method" : "none" } Field client_id Required. Must exactly match the URL the document is served from redirect_uris Required. The redirect_uri in Step 2 must exactly match one of these client_name Shown to the user when they confirm the connection. Defaults to the URL's host grant_types Must include authorization_code . Add refresh_token to receive refresh tokens response_types Must be code if present token_endpoint_auth_method Must be none if present. Client secrets are not supported Grain applies these rules to documents and their clients: The URL must use https and serve the document directly, with no redirects, in at most 5 KB. Grain caches the document for the max-age in its Cache-Control header, between 5 minutes and 24 hours, and revalidates it with its ETag . PKCE is required, so send code_challenge in Step 2 and code_verifier when generating the token. http redirect URIs are only allowed on localhost , 127.0.0.1 and [::1] , where any port matches. The workspace scope is only available to clients verified by Grain. Refresh Token After the access_token has expired, you may generate a new one. See OAuth2 Refresh Token ← Previous Overview Next Versions → On this page Authenticating Calls Token Types OAuth2 Flow Authorization Code Client ID Metadata Document Refresh Token

Export meetings | Grain Skip to main content Developer docs Get started Developer docs Get started Search for articles... All Collections Meetings Export meetings Export meetings Download or export your Grain meetings and transcripts, one at a time, in bulk, or via API. Updated over a month ago Table of contents Whether you're building an AI workflow with your meeting data, migrating to a new tool, or just want your transcripts in a format you can work with elsewhere, Grain gives you several ways to get your data out. The right option depends on how many meetings you need and what you're doing with them. Which option is right for you? What you're trying to do Best option Download one or a few meetings Option 1: Single-meeting download Bulk download transcripts for AI workflows Option 2: Multi-select bulk download Bulk download all meetings in a curated collection Option 3: Playlists bulk export Pipe all workspace meetings to a database or custom AI Option 4: Grain API Query meeting data directly in Claude or ChatGPT Option 5: Grain MCP Option 1: Download a single meeting Use this for one-off downloads when you need a specific meeting's recording or transcript. From the 'Meetings' page: Select the three-dot menu on any meeting card. Select your desired download option: Open in AI: opens your meeting data directly in ChatGPT or Claude. Download transcript for AI: downloads a transcript with metadata for AI. Download recording: downloads an MP4 video of your meeting. Download transcript: downloads the plain transcript text in your desired file format. From inside a meeting: Open the meeting. Click the three-dot icon in the top right. Hover over 'Download' and select your desired download option. Alternatively, inside a meeting, you can: Click the drop-down next to the three-dot icon in the top right. Select your desired download option: Open in AI: opens your meeting data directly in ChatGPT or Claude. Copy/Download transcript for AI: copy or download a transcript with metadata for AI. What you can download Recording — MP4 video file (720p) Transcript — available in Markdown, DOCX, PDF, SRT, or VTT format For more detail on the 'Open in AI' and 'Download transcript for AI' options, including how the transcript is packaged and link expiration, see AI Transcript Actions . Note: Downloading the recording exports the video only. To get the transcript, select 'Download transcript' separately and choose your format. Option 2: Bulk select and download Use this to grab transcripts from multiple meetings at once. Bulk download is limited to 20 meetings at a time. From the 'Meetings' page: On your Meetings page, check the box next to any meeting to enter multi-select mode. Select as many meetings as you want. Choose an action from the bar that appears: Open in AI: combines selected transcripts into a temporary link and opens them in ChatGPT or Claude for analysis. Download: downloads a ZIP file containing Markdown transcripts for all selected meetings. If you've already organized your meetings into a Playlist, you can download all of them without re-selecting: Select the three dots on any Playlist. Use the 'Open in AI' or 'Download' actions available to export your meeting data. Note: The ZIP file contains one Markdown file per meeting. Video recordings are not included. Option 3: Bulk export from a Playlist If you have meetings organized into a Playlist, you can download all transcripts in that Playlist at once, optimized for feeding into an AI tool. 1. Go to 'Playlists' in the left sidebar and open any Playlist. 2. Click the AI actions dropdown arrow at the top of the Playlist. 3. Select 'Download Transcripts for AI'. Grain packages all transcripts in the Playlist into a ZIP folder with a Markdown file for each meeting in the Playlist, ready to paste or upload into any AI tool. See Playlists for more. Option 4: Export via the Grain API Use the API to programmatically extract transcripts and recordings. Personal API token Any user, on every plan including Free, can generate a personal token to access meetings they have permission to view. Go to 'Account settings' → 'Integrations' → 'Personal API'. Click 'Generate personal API token'. Workspace API token (admins only) Workspace admins on Business and Enterprise plans can generate a token with access to all meetings across the workspace. Go to 'Workspace settings' → 'Integrations' → 'API'. Click 'Generate workspace API token'. What you can extract: Transcripts MP4 recordings Rate limit: ~300 API calls per minute. Note: Workspace API tokens provide access to all meetings in your workspace. Only generate one if you're the admin responsible for managing workspace data. For full API reference, see Grain API Documentation Option 5: Use the Grain MCP Use the Grain MCP to query and analyze your meeting data directly inside Claude, ChatGPT, or Cursor. What the MCP can access: Meetings and transcripts Notes and action items Coaching feedback Deal data Clips Setup A workspace admin enables the Grain MCP connector for the workspace. Each user connects their own Grain account via OAuth. Users can only access meetings they already have permission to view in Grain. Example prompt: Pull my 10 most recent meeting transcripts and compile them into a single summary. For each meeting, include: - Meeting title and date - Key decisions made - Action items and who owns them Then identify any themes or topics that came up across multiple meetings. Once connected, you can ask your AI tool to pull transcripts, search meeting content, surface action items, or analyze deal data. Note: The MCP doesn't download files, it lets your AI tool read and search meeting data interactively. Use Options 1, 2, or 3 if you need files to keep or move elsewhere. For full setup instructions, see the Official Grain MCP Server . Next up: Tags Did this answer your question?
